Whether higher bone mineral density (BMD) reflects shared aetiology with or causation of osteoarthritis (OA is unsettled, although people with OA tend to have higher BMD.
Reverse MR was null and underpowered (power 0.14–0.26).
One BMD-raising profile thus protects against fracture yet raises knee-OA risk; the asymmetry rests on the forward estimates, whose overlap-induced bias is bounded at ≤2.6%.

The direction matters clinically: if high BMD predisposes to OA, treatments that increase areal BMD may carry an OA cost — though whether that cost is mediated by bone mass or by skeletal size has not been partitioned.
Three questions remain open.
First, most analyses included at most two BMD sites, so site specificity is unknown, even though OA is joint-localised and BMD is regulated site by site.
Second, OA has usually been represented by a single definition, leaving it unclear whether radiographic OA and self-reported OA relate to bone in the same way.

Harmonisation against each outcome — exclusion of palindromic and strand-ambiguous variants and of instruments absent from the outcome GWAS — reduced the analysed sets to 16–31 instruments per forward pair and 69 per knee-OA-exposure pair; 47 of the 116 knee-OA instruments (41%) were lost at this step, an attrition we report explicitly (Supplementary Fig.
**Sample overlap.** All pairs share UK Biobank participants, partially violating the two-sample assumption.

We report MR-Egger, weighted median and MR-PRESSO alongside IVW and applied an overlap-robust correction (MRlap) [15] to all ten pairs; MRlap moved every estimate further from the null (median 20%), so the primary estimates are conservative with respect to overlap.
Any-fracture correlated negatively with every BMD site (r_g −0.45 to −0.60; all q_FDR<0.001) and positively but non-significantly with both OA definitions (+0.15, +0.21).
Of 78 pairs, 76 were significant at BH-FDR and 75 at Bonferroni; the two OA–fracture pairs were the expected null.
The estimate held under random effects (p=2.4×10⁻¹²), the MR-Egger intercept was null (p=0.558), weighted median agreed (−0.364), and leave-one-out produced no sign reversal.
The femoral-neck set (25 SNPs) gave a concordant result (β=−0.351; OR 1.42, 1.34–1.51); the conservative 1-Mb set gave β=−0.366 (OR 1.44).

Heterogeneity was high (I²=68–86%), and under random-effects IVW only two of five exposures remained significant (total-body p=0.006, lumbar-spine p=0.017); this count depends on the random-effects convention, because a DerSimonian–Laird additive-τ² implementation additionally retains the arms exposure under random effects (p=0.033).

We therefore base the causal reading on the concordance of pleiotropy-robust estimators rather than on fixed-effect p-values; all five effects remained positively causal after MR-PRESSO outlier removal, with four of five strengthening.

**Reverse MR and OA→fracture are null and underpowered.** Knee OA as exposure gave non-significant effects on total-body BMD (β=+0.106, p=0.33), femoral-neck BMD (β=+0.142, p=0.19) and fracture (β=+0.092, p=0.40).
These three estimates were weakly powered (achieved power 0.14–0.26; Table 4), excluding |β|≥0.30 but not moderate effects.

Removing the MR-PRESSO outliers flagged for these pairs moved two of the three point estimates substantially (total-body BMD to +0.171, fracture to +0.200) without altering their non-significance, so the nulls reflect both low power and sensitivity to instrument selection.

**MR-PRESSO and robustness.** The distortion test was significant for 9/10 pairs (expected from high I²) and identified 0–3 outliers per pair; removing outliers did not reverse any direction, and strict-clumped estimates reproduced the conservative 1-Mb clumping.
MRlap confirmed every estimate moved further from the null (median 20%).

One locus fell marginally short: rs11228269 (chr11:68.29 Mb, in the LRP5 region; BMD z=−8.65, knee-OA z=−4.06, direction-concordant) gave PP.H4=0.799, i.e. 0.0006 below the pre-specified threshold, with the residual posterior mass on a BMD-only signal (PP.H1=0.156).

We retain the pre-specified threshold and do not count this as colocalisation, but report it explicitly because the posterior is continuous and the 0.8 cut-off is a convention; a reader applying a 0.75 threshold would read this locus as shared.

The knee-OA null reflects power — under the MR estimate, the expected knee-OA z at the strongest instrument is 0.85, and reaching genome-wide significance would require ~5×10⁷ participants (~42× the present sample).

Because conditioning on height captured a genuine, direct OA-raising height effect (θ_H=+0.043 to +0.049, p≈10⁻¹⁶ to 10⁻¹⁹), the attenuation reflects size confounding, not dilution by a null covariate.
On the pleiotropy-robust evidence, genetically higher BMD raises knee-OA risk; the reverse (OA→BMD) and OA→fracture estimates were non-significant and underpowered.
Subchondral bone sclerosis and osteophyte formation are hallmarks of OA and may share regulatory programs with systemic bone accrual [27–30].

MVMR conditioning on height attenuated the effect by 9.5–33.2%, while the fracture positive control moved only −1.7% to −3.0%, and height itself carried a direct OA-raising effect consistent with established epidemiology [24,25].
This cautions against generalising any single BMD→OA estimate across joints.
We therefore restate P6 as a magnitude claim rather than a directional one, and pre-register the decision rule (a hip effect that is positive and at least as large as the knee's would fail P6).

The set-point is operationalised as areal BMD, a composite of volumetric density and size that we partition only partially here (67–91% height-independent); it is a latent tendency indexed by areal BMD, not a directly measured quantity.

**Strengths and limitations.** Strengths: ten BMD sites with two OA definitions; an internal BMD–fracture positive control calibrated against the published GEFOS estimate (OR 1.40–1.42 vs 1.55); dual FDR/Bonferroni correction; a common SNP set throughout; and directional concordance across IVW, MR-Egger, weighted median and MR-PRESSO.

Limitations: areal BMD conflates size with mass, and although height-conditioning bounds the size-attributable share at 9.5–33.2%, a direct volumetric decomposition is not yet available; heterogeneity is high across all pairs including the positive control, so the causal claim rests on estimator concordance rather than on fixed-effect p-values; the reverse and OA→fracture estimates are null but weakly powered (0.14–0.26), excluding only |β|≥0.30; and residual sample overlap, although bounded at ≤2.6% for BMD→OA and acting in the observed direction, cannot be removed with summary data alone.
